modules.title: Name the whole
modules.desc: Use fraction knowledge to identify what 100% represents.
modules.rule: A percentage is a fraction of a named whole. 25% = 25/100 = 1/4.
teach: The percent sign does not create a new kind of calculation. It writes a fraction on a per-hundred scale.
Start every story with: "100% is ..." The real whole can be 40 children, 80 marks or 800 rupees. It does not have to be 100 objects.
Then name the part. Use P = (p/100) x W. The p is the percentage number; p/100 is the fractional share.
contrast: Same share, different whole, different amount.
modules.transfer: Write two stories in which 25% is 12. What must 100% be in both?
modules.prereq: Start here, even if arithmetic is already fluent.

modules.title: Changed or remaining?
modules.desc: Separate the selected part from its complement.
modules.rule: Changed part + remaining part = the same whole.
teach: A discount is the money removed, not the sale price. A decline is the amount lost, not the amount left.
If p% is removed, (100 - p)% remains. In fraction form, if r = p/100 is removed, 1 - r remains.
For a 20% discount, r = 20/100 = 1/5. The price paid is 1 - 1/5 = 4/5 of the original. Use the complement only when the question asks for the other part.
contrast: Both amounts use the SAME original whole.
modules.transfer: Write two questions about a 90% decrease: one asking for the loss and one asking for what remains.
modules.prereq: First be comfortable naming the whole.

modules.title: Find the percentage
modules.desc: Choose the numerator and the correct reference denominator.
modules.rule: percentage number p = (requested part / reference whole) x 100
teach: First choose the part the question asks about. For a discount percentage, the part is original price minus sale price.
Then decide what 100% is. A discount is measured against the ORIGINAL price, not the reduced price.
Write p/100 = part/whole. This keeps the fractional share separate from the percentage number.
contrast: Rs. 400 is 80% of an original Rs. 500.
The Rs. 100 reduction is 20% of Rs. 500.
The new-price percentage and the discount percentage add to 100%.
modules.transfer: Make a story in which 24 is 30%. Name the whole and show why the denominator is not 24.
modules.prereq: Know which part is being requested.

modules.title: Find the hidden whole
modules.desc: Work backwards when the given amount is only a share.
modules.rule: share x unknown whole = known part
teach: The only amount printed in a story need not be 100%. After a 20% discount, the known price is 80% of the original.
Write the forward relationship first: (80/100) x W = 640. Then undo it: W = 640 / (80/100).
A fraction route is equally good: if 4/5 is 640, then 1/5 is 160 and 5/5 is 800. Or use 1% then 100%.
contrast: Rs. 160 is 20% of WHAT? The whole is Rs. 800.
Adding 20% to a discounted price does not generally restore the original.
modules.transfer: Create a problem where 75% is 90. Solve it through 1/4 rather than through decimals.
modules.prereq: Be secure with the known-whole relationship first.

modules.title: BY is different from TO
modules.desc: Distinguish a change from a final level, including more than 100%.
modules.rule: BY names the change. TO names the new level.
teach: Decreased BY 20% means 80% remains. Decreased TO 20% means 20% remains.
Increased BY 50% means the original 100% plus another 50%: 150% of the original.
More than 100% is possible when comparing a new amount with the old whole. 150% = 3/2 of the original.
contrast: 80 increased BY 50% and TO 150% both become 120.
modules.transfer: Write a BY statement and a TO statement that describe the same increase.
modules.prereq: Understand complementary shares before adding new language.

modules.title: Build a balanced equation
modules.desc: Attach each percentage to its whole and turn words into an equality.
modules.rule: Convert each percentage-of expression into an amount, then keep the equality true.
teach: Two percentages in one question may refer to different wholes. 16% of 150 and 13% of 600 are not shares of the same amount.
Then use ordinary missing-number reasoning: Z + 24 = 78, so Z = 54. In 25% of Z = 40% of 60, the unknown is a whole instead.

Complementary shares can also form an equation: if 60% are girls and 40% are boys, with 12 more girls, then (60/100) x Z - (40/100) x Z = 12. Subtracting these shares is valid because they use the SAME whole.
contrast: Subtract the AMOUNTS: 78 - 24. Do not subtract 13% - 16% across different wholes.
modules.transfer: Make an equality in which 20% of one whole equals 25% of a different whole.
modules.prereq: Be able to find both a part and a hidden whole.

modules.title: Reach a target across tests
modules.desc: Translate overall percentages into totals of marks.
modules.rule: marks already earned + missing score = total marks needed
teach: An overall percentage refers to total earned marks divided by total possible marks. First count the marks available in each group of tests.
Four tests out of 80 give a past maximum of 320. Five tests give a final maximum of 400. Therefore 30% and 35% in this story use DIFFERENT wholes.
Write (30/100) x 320 + Z = (35/100) x 400. That is 96 + Z = 140, so Z = 44 marks. Always check that the required score is possible.
contrast: Final score: 140 - 96 = 44 out of 80, not 5% of 80.
modules.transfer: Explain why a required score greater than the test maximum means the target is impossible under the stated rules.
modules.prereq: Build an equality from two percentage-of expressions.

modules.title: Choose the comparison base
modules.desc: Reverse comparisons and separate percentages from percentage points.
modules.rule: The reference amount determines the denominator.
teach: 100 is 25% more than 80 because the difference 20 is compared with 80. But 80 is 20% less than 100 because the same difference is compared with 100.
A change from 40% to 50% is 10 percentage points. The relative increase is 10/40 = 25%. These are different questions.
Treat this module as optional extension. Always name the requested unit: an amount, a percentage, or percentage points.
contrast: A 10-point rise from 40% is a 25% relative increase.
modules.transfer: Create two reverse percentage comparisons that use the same difference but different denominators.
modules.prereq: Be secure with part/whole and percentage change.

modules.title: Follow a changing whole
modules.desc: Track the new base through successive percentage changes.
modules.rule: Each new percentage uses the whole named for that step.
teach: After a change, the current amount can become the next step's 100%. Label that new reference explicitly.
Start at 100. A 20% decrease leaves 80. A 20% increase OF 80 adds 16, leaving 96. The changes do not cancel because the bases differ.
Write one step at a time, then link them: F = 100 x 0.8 x 1.2. Do not simply add percentage changes on different bases.
contrast: Down 20%, then up 20%, leaves 96% of the original.
modules.transfer: A 20% reduction leaves 80. What percentage increase of 80 would restore 100? Explain the new denominator.
modules.prereq: Understand both BY/TO and comparison bases.

modules.title: Combine unequal groups
modules.desc: Use total parts over total wholes instead of blindly averaging rates.
modules.rule: overall percentage = (sum of parts / sum of wholes) x 100
teach: A test out of 20 and a test out of 80 do not contribute equal numbers of marks. Combine their earned marks and maximum marks, not just their percentage labels.
A simple average of test percentages gives the correct combined-mark percentage when the maximum marks are equal. With unequal maximums, combine the actual marks first.
modules.transfer: Explain why a high score on a very small test may change the overall percentage only a little.
modules.prereq: Understand which quantities form the combined whole.

stages.prompt: Which maximum belongs to each percentage?

options.feedback: Past maximum = 4 x 60 = 240; full maximum = 5 x 60 = 300.
One test is out of this amount, but the percentages in this story refer to groups of tests.
The earlier score refers only to tests already taken.

stages.prompt: What must the last-test score do?

options.text: Marks already earned + last score = total marks needed
options.feedback: The student already has 120 marks and needs 165 in total.

options.text: Last score = target percentage - earlier percentage
options.feedback: The percentage gap is not a score and the two percentages have different totals.

options.text: Last score must be exactly 55% of one test
options.feedback: That would not make up for the earlier scores being below the target.

stages.hint: Model the target as a total, not a percentage gap.

stages.prompt: Let Z be the last-test score. Which equation matches?

options.feedback: This uses the percentage gap on one test rather than balancing the total marks.
The earlier percentage does not apply to all tests.

clinic.title: The discount is not the price paid
clinic.claim: A toy costs Rs. 800 with a 20% discount. "The sale price is Rs. 160."
clinic.right: The changed share was used instead of the remaining share.
wrong: The original price should be the unknown.
20% must be added to the original.
clinic.repair: 20% is 160 saved; 80% is 640 paid. Both shares use the original Rs. 800.
clinic.ask: What is the actual sale price?

clinic.title: Reverse the relationship, not the discount
clinic.claim: After a 20% discount, a bag costs Rs. 640. "The original price is 640 + 20% of 640 = Rs. 768."
clinic.right: The 20% was taken from the reduced price instead of the original whole.
wrong: A discount should use more than 100%.
The child forgot to subtract 20 rupees.
clinic.repair: Rs. 640 represents 80% of W. So (80/100) x W = 640 and W = 800.

clinic.title: Choose the reference denominator
clinic.claim: A price falls from Rs. 10,800 to Rs. 8,640. "The discount is 2,160/8,640 x 100 = 25%."
clinic.right: The discount was compared with the new price, not the original price.
wrong: The numerator should be the new price.
The reduction must be added to 100.
clinic.repair: Discount percentage = 2,160/10,800 x 100 = 20%. The 25% instead describes the increase needed from 8,640 back to 10,800.

clinic.title: A large decrease leaves a small remainder
clinic.claim: A problem starts with 250,000 animals and removes 90%. "225,000 animals remain."
clinic.right: 225,000 is the loss; only the complementary 10% remains.
wrong: 90% should be treated as 90 animals.
The original population is 10% of the remainder.

clinic.title: A percentage gap is not a test score
clinic.claim: Four tests out of 80 have an overall score of 30%. The goal across five is 35%. "The last score must be 5% of 80 = 4."
clinic.right: The earlier and target percentages refer to different total maximums.
wrong: The fifth test is out of 100.
30% means 30 marks in every test.
clinic.repair: Past: 30% of 320 = 96. Target: 35% of 400 = 140. Last score = 44.

clinic.title: Keep each percentage with its own whole
clinic.right: The two percentage numbers were combined despite having different wholes.
wrong: Both percentages must be of 150.
The percent signs should simply be ignored.

clinic.title: Equal percentage changes need not cancel
clinic.claim: An amount starts at 100, decreases by 20%, then increases by 20%. "It returns to 100."
clinic.right: The second 20% is of 80, not of 100.
wrong: A percentage increase is never allowed after a decrease.
Both steps should subtract 20.

clinic.title: Reverse comparison, different base
clinic.claim: A ribbon is 100 cm and another is 80 cm. "The shorter one is 25% shorter than the longer one."
clinic.right: The 20 cm difference was divided by 80 rather than the 100 cm reference.
wrong: The difference should be 180 cm.
The percentage must be greater than 100%.
clinic.repair: Shorter relative to 100: 20/100 x 100 = 20%. The reverse comparison is 25% longer relative to 80.
clinic.ask: What percentage shorter is the 80 cm ribbon than the 100 cm ribbon?

clinic.title: Do not average unequal test weights
clinic.claim: A student scores 18/20 and 40/80. "The overall percentage is (90 + 50)/2 = 70%."
clinic.right: Equal weight was given to tests with unequal maximum marks.
wrong: The smaller test should count twice.
Only the larger test should count.

clinic.title: Points and relative change are different
clinic.claim: A participation rate rises from 40% to 50%. "That is a 10% relative increase."
clinic.right: A 10-percentage-point gap was confused with a relative percentage increase.
wrong: The increase should be divided by the new 50%.
A percentage rate can never itself increase.
clinic.repair: The gap is 10 percentage points. Relative increase = 10/40 x 100 = 25%.
clinic.ask: What is the relative percentage increase?
